subjective.question: What are the two conditions for total internal reflection to occur?
subjective.answer: Total internal reflection takes place when: (1) the ray of light travels from a denser medium to a rarer medium, e.g. from glass or water into air; and (2) the angle of incidence in the denser medium is greater than the critical angle for that pair of media. When both conditions are fulfilled, the ray is not refracted out but is reflected completely back into the denser medium.

subjective.question: What are the effects of anomalous expansion of water?
subjective.answer: Water contracts on cooling down to 4 °C, but on further cooling from 4 °C to 0 °C it expands instead of contracting; this is called the anomalous expansion of water. Its important effects are: (1) water pipes burst in winter because the water inside them expands on freezing; (2) ponds and lakes freeze only at the top — the ice, being less dense, floats and insulates the water below, which stays at about 4 °C, so aquatic life survives under the ice; (3) a bottle completely filled with water may crack when the water freezes; (4) water freezing in the cracks of rocks expands and breaks the rocks apart (weathering).

subjective.question: What is temperature? Give its SI unit. Also discuss the thermometer.
subjective.answer: Temperature is the degree of hotness or coldness of a body. Scientifically, it is the property which determines the direction of flow of heat between two bodies: heat flows from a body at higher temperature to a body at lower temperature. It is related to the average kinetic energy of the particles of a body. The SI unit of temperature is the kelvin (K). A thermometer is an instrument used for measuring temperature. It works on the principle that some physical property of a substance, called the thermometric property, changes uniformly with temperature — for example, the expansion of mercury or alcohol in the capillary tube of a liquid-in-glass thermometer. Common types are the laboratory thermometer and the clinical thermometer, which has a constriction near the bulb that prevents the mercury thread from falling back, and measures from 35 °C to 42 °C.

subjective.question: State Newton's three laws of motion.
subjective.answer: First law (law of inertia): Every body continues in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless it is compelled by an external force to change that state. Second law: The rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the applied force and takes place in the direction of the force, i.e. F = ma. Third law: To every action there is an equal and opposite reaction; action and reaction act on two different bodies.

subjective.question: Write the three equations of motion and define each symbol used.
subjective.answer: For a body moving with uniform acceleration: (1) v = u + at; (2) S = ut + ½at²; (3) 2aS = v² − u². Here u is the initial velocity, v is the final velocity, a is the uniform acceleration, t is the time taken, and S is the distance covered (displacement). These equations are valid only for motion in a straight line with constant acceleration.

subjective.question: Differentiate between distance and displacement, and between speed and velocity.
subjective.answer: Distance is the total length of the path travelled by a body; it is a scalar quantity and is always positive. Displacement is the shortest straight-line distance from the initial to the final position, along with direction; it is a vector quantity and can be positive, negative or zero. Speed is the distance covered per unit time (a scalar), while velocity is the displacement per unit time (a vector). A body moving with uniform speed may still have a changing velocity if its direction changes, e.g. in circular motion.

subjective.question: Define work and power. Give their SI units and state the conditions for work to be done.
subjective.answer: Work is said to be done when a force applied on a body moves the body through some distance in the direction of the force. Work = force × displacement × cosθ, where θ is the angle between the force and the displacement. The SI unit of work is the joule (J). Work is done only when: (1) a force acts on the body, (2) the body is displaced, and (3) the displacement is not perpendicular to the force. Power is the rate of doing work, P = W/t; its SI unit is the watt (W).

subjective.question: What is momentum? State the law of conservation of momentum.
subjective.answer: Momentum of a body is the product of its mass and velocity, p = mv. It is a vector quantity and its SI unit is Ns (kg m/s). The law of conservation of momentum states that if no external force acts on a system, the total momentum of the system remains constant. This law applies to collisions, explosions and recoil phenomena, e.g. the recoil of a gun when a bullet is fired.

subjective.question: Define specific heat capacity. Why does land heat up faster than the sea?
subjective.answer: The specific heat capacity of a substance is the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of the substance by 1 K (or 1 °C). Its unit is J/(kg·K). The specific heat of water is much higher than that of land (soil and sand), so the same amount of solar heat raises the temperature of land much more than that of water. Therefore land heats up faster during the day and also cools down faster at night, while coastal areas have a moderate climate.

subjective.question: Explain the three modes of transfer of heat: conduction, convection and radiation.
subjective.answer: Conduction is the transfer of heat through a solid from its hotter part to its colder part without the actual movement of the particles; the particles only vibrate and pass energy to neighbours, e.g. a metal rod becoming hot at the other end. Convection is the transfer of heat in liquids and gases by the actual movement of the fluid: the heated fluid expands, becomes less dense and rises, while the cooler denser fluid sinks, setting up convection currents, e.g. heating of water in a kettle and sea breeze. Radiation is the transfer of heat in the form of electromagnetic waves (infrared) which needs no material medium, e.g. heat from the Sun reaching the Earth.

subjective.question: State the laws of reflection of light.
subjective.answer: First law: The angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection (∠i = ∠r), both measured from the normal at the point of incidence. Second law: The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane. These laws hold for all types of mirrors — plane, concave and convex.

subjective.question: What is an optical fibre? On what principle does it work? Give two uses.
subjective.answer: An optical fibre is a very thin strand of glass or plastic consisting of a core surrounded by a cladding of lower refractive index. It works on the principle of total internal reflection: light entering the core at a suitable angle strikes the core–cladding boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle and is reflected again and again inside the fibre, emerging at the other end with very little loss. Uses: (1) in telecommunications for transmitting telephone and internet signals; (2) in medicine, in endoscopes, for viewing internal organs of the body.

subjective.question: Why are ionic bonds strong?
subjective.answer: An ionic bond is formed by the complete transfer of electrons from a metal atom to a non-metal atom, producing oppositely charged ions. These positive and negative ions are held together by a strong electrostatic force of attraction and are arranged in a regular three-dimensional crystal lattice. A very large amount of energy, called lattice energy, is required to break this attraction. Hence ionic bonds are strong, and ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points and are hard solids.

subjective.question: What is a chemical bond?
subjective.answer: A chemical bond is the force of attraction which holds two or more atoms together in a molecule or a compound. Atoms form chemical bonds by losing, gaining or sharing electrons in their outermost shells so that each atom achieves a stable electronic configuration like that of a noble gas (complete octet). The main types of chemical bonds are ionic bond, covalent bond and coordinate covalent bond.

subjective.question: Describe Bohr's atomic model.
subjective.answer: Bohr's atomic model (1913) is based on the following postulates: (1) Electrons revolve around the nucleus in certain fixed circular orbits, called shells or energy levels, denoted by K, L, M, N or by numbers n = 1, 2, 3, 4. (2) Each orbit has a definite, fixed amount of energy, and an electron revolving in a permitted orbit does not radiate energy, so the atom remains stable. (3) An electron can jump from a lower orbit to a higher orbit by absorbing a fixed amount of energy, and it emits energy when it falls back from a higher orbit to a lower one; this explains the line spectrum of hydrogen. (4) The angular momentum of the electron in a permitted orbit is an integral multiple of h/2π. Bohr's model successfully explained the stability of the atom and the hydrogen spectrum, though it failed for larger atoms.

subjective.question: Define atomic number and mass number. How do isotopes of an element differ from each other?
subjective.answer: Atomic number (Z) is the number of protons present in the nucleus of an atom; it determines the identity of the element. Mass number (A) is the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus, A = Z + N. Isotopes are atoms of the same element having the same atomic number (same number of protons and electrons) but different mass numbers because they contain different numbers of neutrons. They have the same chemical properties but different physical properties (atomic weights), e.g. carbon-12 and carbon-14.

subjective.question: Differentiate between ionic and covalent bonds.
subjective.answer: An ionic bond is formed by the complete transfer of one or more electrons from one atom to another, generally between a metal and a non-metal; the resulting compounds are hard crystalline solids with high melting points, and they conduct electricity in the molten state or in solution but not as solids. A covalent bond is formed by the mutual sharing of electrons between two atoms, generally between non-metals; covalent compounds are usually gases, liquids or soft solids with low melting and boiling points, and they do not conduct electricity. In a coordinate covalent bond, both shared electrons are donated by a single atom.

subjective.question: Write three physical properties each of metals and non-metals.
subjective.answer: Metals: (1) They are hard, lustrous (shiny) solids at room temperature (except mercury, which is a liquid). (2) They are good conductors of heat and electricity. (3) They are malleable and ductile, i.e. they can be beaten into sheets and drawn into wires, and they are sonorous. Non-metals: (1) They are generally dull and exist as gases or brittle solids (except bromine, a liquid). (2) They are bad conductors (insulators) of heat and electricity, except graphite. (3) They are neither malleable nor ductile; solid non-metals are brittle and break when hammered.

subjective.question: What is metallurgy? Name the main steps involved in the extraction of a metal from its ore.
subjective.answer: Metallurgy is the science and process of extracting metals from their naturally occurring ores and refining them for use. The main steps are: (1) mining of the ore; (2) crushing and grinding of the ore; (3) concentration (enrichment) of the ore to remove gangue (earthy impurities), e.g. by froth flotation; (4) extraction of the metal by reduction of the concentrated ore, e.g. by carbon reduction, electrolysis or roasting and smelting as in the blast furnace for iron; (5) refining (purification) of the impure metal, e.g. by electrolysis.

subjective.question: What is an alloy? Give two examples along with their uses.
subjective.answer: An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of a metal with another metal or a non-metal, prepared to improve the properties of the metal, such as hardness, strength and resistance to corrosion. Examples: (1) Stainless steel — iron mixed with chromium and nickel; it does not rust and is used for utensils, cutlery and surgical instruments. (2) Brass — copper mixed with zinc; it is hard and resistant to corrosion and is used for making utensils, taps, locks and musical instruments.
